utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: A very good morning to everybody. Please be seated. And I have to inform you that for serious illness, Judge Mumba is unable to sit today; therefore, we have to discuss whether or not to apply Rule 15 bis, in principle providing for the possibility to continue after the last change of the Rules for a period of not more than five working days. But before we discuss this question, may I ask the registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-94-2-S, the Prosecutor versus Dragan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution today, appearances the same as before; I'm Upawansa Yapa, appearing with Ms. Patricia Sellers and Mr. William Smith, and Diane Boles continues as case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Good morning. Howard Morrison and Tanja Radosavljevic for the accused, Dragan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And may I ask Mr. Nikolic, can you follow the proceedings in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any submissions by the parties whether or not to continue under Rule 15 bis? The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So far as the Prosecution is concerned, we have no objections to the proceedings continuing -- continuing today in the absence of Judge Mumba. Actually, it is my learned friend's day, so it will be more for him to say as to what his stand is. I thank Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we hear the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we're all sorry, of course, to hear of the Judge's incapacity and hope that she recovers as quickly as possible. But I am very disquieted about the possibility of continuing in her absence at this extremely critical moment, as far as the defendant is concerned. This isn't a question simply, of course, of reading what are non-contentious documents. It's a question of seeing, in the flesh, the only Defence witnesses, and the defendant himself, at really the pivotal point in the Defence case, as far as he is concerned. The only analogy is I can really make is with my own system: It's like losing four out of the eight -- 12 jurors at a critical moment in the Defence case. If it would suffice for jurors simply to see a video and read a transcript, then there would be almost no point in having live hearings in any case, especially when the witnesses come from afar. One would simply video them at home and bring them to court, if that was thought to be a -- as fair a proceeding as could be devised. It's plainly not thought to be as fair a proceeding as could be devised, which is why we've set up this hearing and brought the witnesses in person. And I hope Your Honours take the view that the Defence in this case has not been obdurate or uncooperative, and I don't want to be obdurate or uncooperative, but likewise, I am very disquieted about the possibility of continuing in the absence of Judge Mumba today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just two minutes, please. You have seen that we have discussed your points, and no doubt there are some merits in your suggestion; however, as the underlying principle in this court, why we have changed in the last plenary Rule 15 bis in several parts, allowing to continue even without the consent of the accused when a Judge has to be replaced and, on the other hand, to add -- to prolong the period from three days to five working days; the underlying reasons was -- and this was a clear result of the discussion in the plenary. The rationale for this is that opposed to other domestic cases, we don't have only the transcripts, we have in addition the video. And please be assured that the Judges exercise their work very conscientiously. For example, for a certain reason we asked that a video of yesterday's hearing be provided for us that we can check what actually happened. It gives a better impression, and we can recall better what is happening in court. This is, by the way, an extremely good example how difficult it is to rely on witnesses when out of three Judges the one or the other believes to have seen this and the other believes to have seen that. Then we have the video and can check it. It's more reliable. So therefore, it is the rule rather than the exception to continue. We are prepared, in light of the importance of a maybe testimony or statement of your client - we don't know yet - to postpone it and try, if you so want, to hear the statement or the testimony the last possible day this week in order that also Judge Mumba, in case she is well again, can follow this testimony or statement. Can we -- one alternative would have been to continue with the testimony of -- the expert testimony of Dr. Grosselfinger, but I just got the message that in principle she would not be prepared. We can come back to this issue after the break, after a discussion. So we have finally decided to continue under Rule 15 bis with the caveat that it's for you to decide whether to call your client if you so wish for a statement or for a formal testimony. But the presentation and the -- should be given today, and the other witnesses of the Defence should be heard today in the light of that what I have said before on the technical equipment and development that allows Judge Mumba to follow the hearings in a reliable way. So therefore, we will proceed under Rule 15 bis today. May I then ask, as I did yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What is planned for -- what is the agenda of today, in the light of this development?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as far as the Defence is concerned, the only difference in the planned agenda, which is as follows: I am going to make the briefest of openings for the Defence because it's a case which requires a brief and succinct opening for the Defence. It is not one that requires a convoluted opening. The matters in mitigation are going to be presented outside, as it were, the ambit of my speech but with -- included, of course I'm going to make reference to them. I'm going to save the most part of what I say for the final speech, which -- and there is no merit in repetition; it would otherwise become repetition. So today, in the light of the Trial Chamber's ruling, I shall first be making a very short opening. I shall then be calling Mr. Jovo Delic, who is the brother-in-law of the defendant. I anticipate that his evidence will take something in the order of 30 minutes. I do not anticipate, although I'm often proved wrong, that it will generate much in the way of cross-examination from my learned friend, but it may generate some questions from Your Honours. Likewise, I then turn to call Ms. Ljiljana Rikanovic, who's a cousin of the defendant. She can only speak as to post-1996, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just -- okay. Now it's continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: And likewise, I wouldn't have thought that her testimony was going to take much in excess of 30 minutes, certainly as far as the Defence is concerned. It was the intention discussed and thought about and confirmed only this morning indeed that the defendant himself would then not make a statement but give testimony on the issue of remorse and apology or the joint issues of remorse and apology, but in the light of the -- what's happened today, I will first need to speak to him again; and secondly, it may well be the case that having done so, that it is thought better to wait until the last day of the hearing, when hopefully Judge Mumba will be recovered from her illness. That really is the -- the layout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this. As we already indicated, we would understand if you would postpone, however, I would like -- I can see that Dr. Grosselfinger is following, as it was indicated in the scheduling order of the proceedings, in the public gallery. We would kindly ask her to review and revisit her thoughts whether or not after a reasonable break she can -- she can be prepared to answer questions that may arise from her expertise. We have the expertise already in writing before us, and we have all studied it, so it would be limited to additional questions, and it would be only a short intervention. For this reason, I would ask Dr. Grosselfinger - I hope she can follow us - to revisit this question and be prepared to answer this question immediately during -- after the first break we will have, say, in three-quarters from now. I can't promise that Judge Mumba - and it's really unforeseeable - that she will be ready for trial during this week. The Defence should take this into account. She seems to be seriously ill. And in the light of this, we have to be extremely flexible, and I and the entire Bench, we of course understand your considerations, but please also understand that we have to be as expeditious as possible. Thank you for this understanding, and may I ask you to start your opening remarks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm grateful. On a simply procedural matter, it may be useful - I don't know - in the light of the illness of Judge Mumba and in the light of the possible changes to the considered and scheduled layout of the case - I don't know; I'm simply thinking aloud - that it might be better if we had a short Rule 65 ter meeting today at the conclusion of whatever evidence we hear today so that we can plan the rest of the week consensually. I'd simply throw that suggestion in for all parties to consider. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can see no objections from the Prosecution, and as we have also to discuss a serious legal issue we were aware of only yesterday, it's indeed appropriate to have immediately after the hearing - let's see how long it will take us - a 65 ter (I) meeting in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I interject only to say I already have such a meeting in another matter of that scheduled at -- at the moment at 2.30, but I think that's probably a movable feast. But that can be determined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So thank you for this suggestion. We will follow this. And please start.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I have said that I'm going to be brief, and I am. The Defence case is in one sense simple. It always is when an accused person has pleaded guilty to the indictment that he faces. As we all know, some people sometimes plead partially guilty to an indictment; they negotiate the pleas; they extract from the Prosecution in fact a deal in the sense of do not pursue me on Counts 1 to 5 and I will plead guilty to Counts 6 to 10 or something of that nature. The reality in this case is that, although the indictment has been substantially reduced in size, it's not really been substantially reduced in content, which only goes to show how a little careful thought can reduce an unwieldy document into one that is relatively simple. And for that reason I say the guilty plea is simple. It's straightforward in the sense that the accused has admitted his guilt and he's admitted very serious offences, and there's no gainsaying that. He knows that better than anyone else. But in another sense, it's complex. And now I look at the accused himself. And even what we've heard so far raises mysteries. It's going to be, I anticipate, the unchallenged evidence that prior to 1992 the defendant was an ordinary - and I don't mean that in a disparaging sense - an ordinary, hard-working man from a relatively small town, who knew the community and town well and the community knew him. And the evidence I anticipate will show that he is a person who is a -- engaged in sports, like most young men did, had girlfriends, as most young men do, had a reasonably steady work record, which not every young man does, unhappily, but he did; had no criminal record whatsoever; and until the horrors that embroiled the Balkans, he was probably going to live an unremarkable life; perhaps get married, perhaps have children, more likely than not simply settle down in Vlasenica and raise a family. If one was a betting man, one would put money on that being the scenario which would have unfolded and developed. But we know that didn't happen, and that's where the complexity lies. It's not suggested by the Prosecution properly and rightly that this defendant was in any way a prime mover in what happened in the Balkans. He wasn't a high-ranking political figure; indeed, he was not a political figure at all. He wasn't a high-ranking military officer. Indeed, he never advanced beyond -- in the 1992 conflict that, effectively, of a private soldier. And yet, of course, he accepts and understands not only through his plea to the indictment but through his own cognisance now of what happened all those years ago, 11 years ago, that such conflicts are made up in the first part usually of politics; in the second part, and intertwined with politics so you cannot distinguish one from the other, nationalism; and in the third part, human emotion, which operates on a wide social basis but more particularly on an individual basis. And the only sense that I can advocate for his behaviour during the three months that we are concerned with at Susica camp is that this was a man who could not cope with the demands that were made upon him and placed upon him by others, that the dark side of his character, which hitherto had not even begun to show itself, emerged, and he did things which in normal circumstances - and the circumstances in 1992 were far from normal - in normal circumstances which would never have arisen. And as I said, he would have just been - I hope he understands that I say this with respect - an ordinary man. His story - if I may use the literary analogy - would have been the rattle of a simple man. And that's where it becomes complex; how does somebody who is otherwise an ordinary, law-abiding, socially acceptable, likable person do these things and then stop doing them and then years later face up to them? And that's part of the -- the mystery of this case. So it starts off in one way as being simple. It then gets rather more complicated. And perhaps - now, this is where the report of Dr. Grosselfinger comes in - it's only really easy to understand or easier to understand the complexities of the second part if you are used to doing so and you have an academic and professional background which assists you in doing so. We can all understand the common-sense argument of men being given guns in uniforms doing bad things. History is littered with those examples. But there is then a third element to that. You take the simplicity, you take the complexity, and then you take the third, which is the last chapter, and that's hope. And hope derives in this case in three particular ways: First because the defendant has pleaded guilty; secondly, because he is going to be demonstrated and has in a sense already been demonstrated as very remorseful; and thirdly, what he is going to do in the future encapsulates the purpose of this Tribunal, which is reconciliation and hope for the future, because without people accepting what they've done and pleading guilty to it, there really is very little hope for the future. Any bad person who commits offences and refuses to admit them underlines his badness. He remains obdurate. There is no real hope for society if any criminal came to the courts, fought their trial to the bitter end, were convicted, imprisoned, never pleaded guilty and never showed remorse. The criminal justice system then would simply be down to locking people up and not to solving the problems of society. And any criminal system, in particular the ad hoc tribunals in the international sense, have a mandate to go further than that and can only go further than that when people see what they have done is wrong, plead guilty to it, are punished for it, and then proceed further in their lives to make it better. Now, that's the structure of the Defence case. To illustrate those points, there will be -- there's some written evidence, not only of course from the Defence but from the -- in a way from the Prosecution as well. There is the expert evidence we've yet to come to. But now I call the two witnesses that the Defence is intending to call today to further illustrate parts of what I have -- and I call, please, Mr. Jovo Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I understand the Defence doesn't want to have any protective measures for one of the witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Delic. Thank you for coming to The Hague as a witness. May I ask you, please, to give your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. The floor is for the Defence. Questioned by Mr. Morrison:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give the Court, please, your full name and your address where you now live -- or just the town and place where you live.

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: My name is Jovo Delic. I was born in Vlasenica on the 19th of March, 1954.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us, please, what your relationship is with the defendant, Dragan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Dragan Nikolic is my brother -- no, in fact, I am his brother-in-law. I've known him for at least 25 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we know he is now 47 years of age, so it follows you knew him from when he was in his early to mid-20s; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you come to meet him for the first time?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Well, I came to know Dragan Nikolic and his family because our families were friends. Our fathers worked together for the same company, so we knew each other from as long as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you socialise with him?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I spent time with him because I worked on a cultural hall where Dragan Nikolic often came to see theatre plays, and there was also a youth club there where young people gathered, never distinguishing among ethnicities. Everybody socialised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you're slightly older than your brother-in-law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: I am four years older than Dragan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But not so much older that you wouldn't have social interests in common.

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. We socialised in Vlasenica because we were not too far apart in age. Vlasenica is a small town, and young people aged around 20 socialised all together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned at the -- a moment ago in your evidence that you never distinguished between ethnicities. We know from the statistics that before the 1992 conflicts there were, in fact, more Muslims than non-Muslims in Vlasenica. Did you realise that at the time, before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. The composition of the population in Vlasenica was as follows: 60 per cent of Muslims and 30 per cent of Serbs. In those times, we never paid attention to each other's ethnicity. We were simply friends. We didn't distinguish between ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from your observations, did Dragan Nikolic socialise with Muslims as well as people from a Serbian background?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Right. I can say that he, as well as I and all the rest of us, had more friends among Muslims than among Serbs. Some of his best friends were Muslims, who worked together with him and spent time with him socially. I also know that Dragan was a member of the scouts club, the mountaineering club, and they went together on trips to other towns in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those clubs were mixed. There was no distinction between one ethnicity and another, as far as the club was concerned.

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Exactly. Nobody ever mentioned or thought about ethnicities. The question never arised at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thinking back now, now that you've reached a mature age, thinking back now to Dragan as he was in his 20s and 30s, how would you describe him as a man? Give a brief description of him as a man, as a person.

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Well, well, he was very sociable, very communicative. He was never involved in any incidents. He never had a record at the MUP of Vlasenica, and that is verifiable. He was never given to getting involved in trouble. He was never a troublemaker, and he's known as a quiet, decent person by both Serbs and Muslims and Croats. His conduct was quite normal. He never caused any trouble. He was never involved in any incidents on ethnic grounds or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what of his -- as far as you were aware, what of his emotional life? Most young men or many young men have girlfriends and mix with people of the opposite sex. From your own observations, did you see him engaging in that sort of social activity?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Dragan Nikolic did not live in the same street as I did. And when he would go out in the evening to the cinema, for instance, he would always be in the company of girls from his neighbourhood, and he had a girlfriend, as all the other young men did, at that time. However, he had a number of family tragedies; the first one was the loss of his father, who died when he was still very young.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think it's in dispute that Dragan Nikolic was 23 years of age when his father very suddenly and unexpectedly died. Is that your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that his father died very young, and his mother was left alone with three children who needed to be raised and put through school. He was the eldest child. And despite all these difficulties and hardships, he managed to finish school and enrol in university. However, he had to abandon his studies because he could not afford them, and out of those three children he was the first one to get a job to be able to support the others. Later on he thought, when his sister and his brother were graduating from high school and his brother enrolled in university, his brother couldn't go through with his studies either because there was no money for it, and one of the three children had to find a job to support the others. Dragan was, however, more anxious to find a job for his sister because that seemed easier; whereas, he would do odd jobs, until he found permanent employment. And that's what happened. He eventually found a job, and I think that he went back to the university parallel with his job, and I think he read one-year course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the -- again, it's -- I don't think it's in contention that the defendant worked in a -- an aluminium construction factory in Vlasenica called Alpro; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he held a regular and responsible job in that organisation.

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. He found employment in the aluminium coating factory in Vlasenica, where he was the senior warehouse worker, which is a job that carries with it great responsibility, because the warehouse holds very expensive material, and he performed it very well. You can check that with the management at the factory. You can send somebody to make inquiries about his record. At the Alpro factory, the workforce was half/half, I think; half of the employees were Serbs, half were Muslims. But nobody paid attention to that at that time. Everybody socialised normally with everyone else. We really did not distinguish between ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned briefly his immediate family. His father died, leaving the mother with, I think, two boys - Dragan and Milan - and his sister, who you came to marry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of the marriage with the sister, you've had three children, all female children, a set of twins and an older girl; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, and I forgot to say earlier of course I'm married, I have three children. Two of them are twins and the eldest is two years older than the twins.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: And I can only add that Dragan Nikolic has never seen my girls. He wouldn't be able to recognise them in the street if he saw them now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That brings me on to the -- my next question. We know, and it's not contested, that Dragan Nikolic left Vlasenica in 1996 and went to Serbia; you were aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Dragan left for Serbia in 1996, carrying a small plastic bag. His health condition was very bad at the time. He went to live with his uncle in Serbia mostly to get proper treatment, which was unavailable in Vlasenica at the time after the war, and he was at a loss what to do after the war because no one from the official authorities called to tell him, to inform him that he was indicted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you first become aware that there was an indictment from this Tribunal in respect of Dragan Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: I found out from media reports sometime in end 1994 or early 1995. We learnt from the press and the media that Dragan Nikolic had been indicted and charges were levelled against him related to that locality, to that place where he used to work. And we in the family found it hard to believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You found that out, as you say, at the end of 1994, beginning of 1995. But Dragan Nikolic left Vlasenica in 1996. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Dragan left in 1996, and about what I just said, until then he moved around as usual. He was not hiding. But nobody offered any advice. Nobody told him what he was supposed to do. The authorities never approached him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your recollection, was he still living in the family house at that stage in Vlasenica, where he'd always lived?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. He lived as usual at his home, as before. He would go out to town as before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned his brother, called Milan. I think again this is not contested that Milan's body was found upon the grave of this father sometime after Dragan Nikolic had left Vlasenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Another tragedy happened in his family. His brother Milan, I mean, they were very attached to one another. They helped each other. But when Milan heard about these charges and when the media campaign started, when the newspapers started writing all sorts of things and television broadcast all sorts of things, he couldn't take it any longer. He committed suicide on their father's grave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall now what year that was?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: I think it was in 1998. I'm not quite -- 1997, 1998, something like that. I know that it was the month of February. It was wintertime, and we found him up there. He had gone all rigid, lying dead on his father's grave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, once the defendant had left Vlasenica and gone to live in Serbia, what sort of contact did you personally have with him?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Well, when Dragan went to Serbia, while his late brother was still alive, he mostly contacted him over the telephone, things like that. I knew that he had gone to Serbia, but I knew that he had gone for treatment. He called me at times. He called me once from the hospital because he was in a very serious situation then. He had gone numb and he went to a spa for treatment, so his late brother, Milan, is the one who had the biggest number of contacts with him. He's the one who took care of him. And his sister had contacts with him too, but we could not help him financially because my situation is very difficult. The general situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina has been difficult ever since the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you first become aware that the defendant was in The Hague, having been arrested?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: We found out from Dragan Nikolic himself. We found out that he had been abducted from Serbia and he telephoned us and told us that he was in prison, in the prison of The Hague Tribunal, and this caused a feeling of tragedy in the family, especially on the part of his mother and sister. The first time he called, I think he didn't even know where he was at all. Psychologically he was totally dead, if that's how it's usually put, that kind of feeling. We didn't know what to do at the time. We didn't have any money to retain a lawyer, a defence lawyer. We didn't know what to do then. However, thanks to people from the judiciary, from the Tribunal, they retained a lawyer. As you know, Howard Morrison, Mr. Howard Morrison, later on he greatly helped the psychological recovery of Dragan by way of his visits here in prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your contacts - and I think I can lead you on this; I'll be stopped if there's any objection - your contacts with Dragan Nikolic, since he's been in The Hague, have been by phone, letter, and indeed personal visits; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. The only contact we had was when Dragan would phone from The Hague, and then we would chat for about a minute or two. The next contact was the following: My little girls and his sister and his mother all wrote letters, because we are not in a position to visit Dragan here in The Hague. Financially, this is impossible for us. It is impossible for us to come and visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you have, in fact, been able to make a visit -- two visits to him, I think -- in The Hague over the years that he's been there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to take this opportunity to thank the International Red Cross from Geneva that made one of these visits possible. As for the other visit, we had to save up for about a year in order to make it possible to come and visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what changes have you noticed, if any, through your contact with Dragan Nikolic since the time he's been in detention, between -- before he pleaded guilty and after he pleaded guilty? Are you in a position to assist with that?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Well, at the first moment, when he was indicted, Dragan was in a very difficult situation psychologically. Later on, as we he worked with the gentleman lawyer, Dragan became more and more stable psychologically, which can be concluded on the basis of his telephone calls, whenever he called. The more times the lawyer, Mr. Howard, visited him, he was more stable and stable psychologically. As for later - I think that was part of your question too - when he confessed, when he admitted what he admitted. You could feel that he was relieved of his burden and that he had therefore become a different kind of person himself. That is what I observed while we spoke over the telephone. Psychologically he seems to be far more disburdened now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, inevitably he faces a prison sentence, a custodial sentence. I'd simply like to ask you a common-sense question. During the course of that imprisonment and thereafter, will he still have the support, as much as you can give it, of yourself and your family?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. We shall support Dragan while he is in prison, while he serves his sentence. We will also support him when he returns to Vlasenica, God willing, because the times are different now. I think there will be no problem in terms of his return. The people, the ordinary people, have understood what this unfortunate war of 1992 was all about. So Dragan will not have any problems, as far as the other side is concerned; I mean the Bosniak side. When I left in order to come here, many of his friends, Bosniaks, sent their regards. And as for support, we are going to write letters to him at least while he's serving his sentence. Financially, I'm not sure how much support we'll be able to provide, but we'll try to collect something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you just wait there, please, in case there are other questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrison. May I ask the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you'll bear we me for two minutes while I consult.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, Ms. Sellers will ask a few questions, one or two questions. Questioned by Ms. Sellers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Delic. Thank you for coming here and assisting us with the sentencing hearing. As Mr. Yapa has just said, I have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you are the brother-in-law of Mr. Nikolic, and that means you are married to Mr. Nikolic's baby sister; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to having a family relationship with Mr. Nikolic, I understand that you are also an investigator on Mr. Nikolic's Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As part of your responsibilities as an investigator, you have been trying to find evidence to show that Mr. Nikolic might have been innocent of the charges of which he was accused; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, was that a paid position, the investigator for Mr. Nikolic's case?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Investigator's pay is regulated, I think, by your own rules and regulations, so yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you were paid to be the investigator; that's correct, Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. But even if I had not been paid, I would have done it free of charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's because you do care dearly for Mr. Nikolic as his brother-in-law; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: No. First and foremost, I want the truth to be known, and I want a man's name to be cleared, a man who is probably charged with having done things that he had not done. Quite simply, to prove the truth and also to prevent any such thing from ever happening again, things like those that happened in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you understand, Mr. Delic, that Mr. Nikolic right now has admitted to the things to which he was charged were things that he did do?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, you understand that Mr. Nikolic went to Serbia after the events at Susica camp. Were you aware that while in Serbia he lived under false identities?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. As I said to you a few minutes ago, he went to Serbia because nobody had contacted him officially, that is, municipal or state authorities or international authorities, nobody brought him a piece of paper while he was still in Vlasenica. Nobody took a piece of paper to his home stating that he had to report to The Hague Tribunal. So the man simply went to Serbia for medical treatment, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, you mentioned that you brought greetings from Mr. Nikolic's Bosniak friends. I would just like to ask you: As of now, what is the percentage of Bosniaks that live in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Vlasenica, the return has been evolving as a normal procedure. There are about 100 families there, but all the houses belonging to Bosniaks in Vlasenica are free, so they are returning as a matter of course. But the only problem is that there are no jobs, so they have nothing to live on. But if they could get jobs, they would come back; there is no trouble, no incidents, no problem. So the main problem is employment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Bosniak friends of Mr. Nikolic that sent their greetings, were they Bosniaks who were in the camp at Susica when he was a commander?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I don't know how you treat him, but he was no commander. He was just an ordinary guard. The people who sent their greetings, I don't know exactly -- perhaps I can give you their names and surnames in closed session and then you can call these people and ask them and check this out. Once I give you the names, I think it will be easy to check all of this out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no further questions. Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, you stated what we hear nearly in all the cases, that prior to the conflict and prior to the war people lived together irrespective of their ethnicity, and this was also true for Mr. Nikolic and there were no special problems. You mentioned the time period prior to 1990 and then following 1994. May I ask you, have you been in contact with Mr. Nikolic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I did not have any contact with Dragan because I was - I can tell you this quite freely, and you know that yourselves - I was a soldier of the army of Republika Srpska and I went to the front line. I was an ordinary soldier, so I was not in town. We perhaps saw each other once in a month or two in town when I was off, when I was not in the zones of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever on one of these occasions visit Mr. Nikolic in the Susica detention camp?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: No, never. Because there was no need for me to go down there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And just one final question. On page 22 of today's transcript, you stated that you worked as an investigator to find the truth on what really happened during the relevant period of time and that you were paid for this work as an investigator. May I ask, who paid you for these investigations?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Well, probably The Hague Tribunal. I don't know. I don't know exactly what the rules are that you have, in respect of people who do these investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who ordered you to do these investigations?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Well, I was told to do this by Mr. Howard, the lawyer, that I could work and that I could be on this team, because practically Mr. Howard was working on his own. In the beginning, no one was out there with him in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When you received the money, from whom did you get the money?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Well, the money went according to the normal procedure. I got the money like the other investigators get their money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please be more clear on this question.

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is a timetable that is given, and then one has to put in a certain number of hours, and then to provide adequate documents for this, so all of this has to be given to the lawyer, Mr. Howard in this case. And then, since he was the one that was coming here, then he did everything else that was necessary, in terms of administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you saw yourself more or less in the role of part of the team of the Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO DELIC
utterances.text: Well, that would be about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. Judge Agius? No questions. No questions --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just express my thanks to you, Your Honours, for having asked me to come. On behalf of the Nikolic family, on behalf of his mother and his sister, I would like to say that they all offer their apologies in Dragan's case and they would not want this ever to happen again, so they extend their apologies to all people and to all their families, all of those who were victims on the Bosniak side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this, Mr. Delic. May I ask, are there any additional questions from the parties? This seems not to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you. Then we all have to thank you, Mr. Delic, for coming to The Hague and give us some insight in the personality of Mr. Nikolic and his growing up in Vlasenica and the tragic events that happened in those years. And we all hope that in the future once again the ethnicities will be able to live peacefully together. And if you can bring this message back to your home country, that this Tribunal does whatever possible to come as soon as possible to a reconciliation, knowing, however, how difficult this procedure will be after all that what has happened. Thank you very much for coming, and have a safe trip home. The trial stays adjourned until ten minutes to 11:00. Maybe it will take a little bit longer because we have to settle some administrative matters in the meantime, but then we will let you know. But please be prepared that we will continue ten minutes to 11:00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Morrison, before you continue, may I just give some information. During the break, Dr. Grosselfinger was kind enough to declare her readiness in principle to give her expertise today, however, with the caveat that she was only prepared for testifying on Thursday. So in case there would be a question from one of the parties, she's not prepared to answer without having the additional documents at hand. She would ask for continuation on Thursday. I think this is a compromise we all can live with, and therefore we can start at least with hearing her expert testimony today. May we then proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I'm sure I speak for my learned friend as well that we welcome the opportunity to save time by calling Dr. Grosselfinger. And indeed, it won't actually -- from what's been said, it won't actually take any more time because it simply adjourns the question of-- of her answering questions to another day. Overall, I don't see it's going to take any more time from our schedule. One thing I do want to deal with though, because it was raised during the course of cross-examination of Mr. Delic and I'm not happy to let it pass unexplained. When the Defence team wanted to have an investigator based in Vlasenica, the people who were available in Vlasenica who were suitable fell into an extremely small category. It had to be somebody who was trusted by the family, trusted by the defendant, and knew Vlasenica and knew the surrounding district, and more importantly knew and was trusted by the local community from all ethnic backgrounds. Having met Mr. Delic on a visit to Vlasenica, I formed the view that he was an ideal candidate. When I came back to The Hague, I raised this with Mr. Christian Rohde, who was then the head of OLAD, the Office of Legal Aid and Defence, disclosed to Mr. Rohde the relationship between Mr. Delic and the accused, and gave a request that he be assigned to the Defence team as an investigator for limited purposes. That was considered by the Registry. Permission was granted for Mr. Delic to be so engaged, he was so engaged. He did the work that was required of him. He produced the paperwork. I looked at it. I was satisfied that he had done what he had said he had done; indeed, it seemed to me that he had done more than he had said he had done in terms of work and hours spent. I authorised it. I sent it to OLAD, and it was duly authorised and then sent to the accountants, who also duly authorised it. It was all proper, above board, and he was paid the standard rate for an investigator. And I would welcome if anyone has any queries to that to see me later about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation, but I think we shouldn't waste time with side aspects of the case, and it sounds reasonable what you just explained, and therefore it's not for this case to go into any further details of this question. Thank you for this. Do you want to call now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I do, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- your second witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Ljiljana Rikanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Rikanovic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you first for coming to The Hague. And may we please hear your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. And as you are called as a Defence witness, Mr. Morrison, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Questioned by Mr. Morrison:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give the Trial Chamber, please, your full name and your brief personal circumstance, where you live and what you are currently doing.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Ljiljana Rikanovic. I live in Batajnica. I'm unemployed. I live with my family, my sister, my mother, father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is your relationship with the defendant, Dragan Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a relative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Relatives fall into many categories. How do you come to be related to him?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: My father and his mother are half siblings, so he's not so closely related to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I may be wrong about this, but it seems that that makes you some species of cousin to him, perhaps a second cousin. But in any event, he's a family member in the extended sense of the family.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I hope it's not thought impolite, but how old are you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, of course, we are here in the case dealing with matters that happened some 11 years ago, when you would have been about 20. That's not a question as much as an observation. When did you first become aware of the existence of Dragan Nikolic? Can you recall how old you were?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: I was a small child. I don't know, maybe two or three years old. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what's your earliest recollection of actually meeting him? In what circumstances was that?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't see each other often. In fact, we saw each other very rarely, on family occasions. He lived in Vlasenica, we lived in Belgrade. And those were brief visits, family visits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it the case that you really only got to know him as a personality after he'd left Vlasenica, which we know was in 1996, and gone to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That is when I really met him, when I got to know him really, and I'm glad I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that's about eight years ago, so you would have been in your early 20s then. You talked of a sister. You mentioned a sister. How old is she?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Twenty-seven. She's four years younger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does she also live with you and your parents at home?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, she does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so when Dragan Nikolic came to Serbia, she would have, as it were, come across him at the same time that you did; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as well as being able to tell us about your own relationship and observations of Dragan Nikolic, therefore is it true that you can tell us -- only from your observations, of course -- how he appeared to you to relate to your sister?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: The same as to me. He treated us all equally, my sister, me, my father, my mother, everyone who came to visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say he treated you equally. In what way did he treat you?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Very decently. He's a wonderful man. I did not know him before, and I only got to know him then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I understand that when he first came -- do you want to use the tissues there?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he first came to Serbia in 1996, I understand that initially he lived with you in your father's house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he lived with us. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: We lived in a small, old house, all of us together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Five people in all?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Right. Before that, our grandmother used to live with us. And after that, she left for Bosnia and we stayed. But we shared the yard with our tenant -- in fact, tenants. They are a family of refugees who at that time had a very young baby. But we all lived as one family. But speaking of our house alone, we were there alone, our family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did the defendant live with you and your family in those circumstances, from 1996 onwards?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I think it may have been two and a half years. I'm not sure. At the time when he left, we were somewhere on the coast, and I can't say exactly, but I think it was two and a half years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do I interpret this correctly that he left your home in Serbia when you were personally away from Serbia and, therefore, were not aware of exactly when he left?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's the reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for that period of time, be it two or two and a half years, were you seeing the defendant on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: On a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just give us a -- take a typical day, if you can. What would you do? What would he do? How would you interact with each other?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Living with him was wonderful. We were friends. We had long Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. conversations about all sorts of things. We liked to walk and we took walks together. He would often ask me to give him books to read, and I would borrow them from my girlfriends and give them to him. He helped us because we were building a new house at the time, and he was helping us all the time, all the time that he lived with us. Anything that needed to be done, he did anything that he could have done for us. He did -- he never said no, to me, to my sister, or to my mother. He never refused anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what sort of contact were you able to have with him after he left your family home but before he came to The Hague? Were you able to stay in contact with him in that period?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: We never wanted to stop our contact with him, nor did he want to stop being in touch with us. And when he left, we missed him a lot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to -- sorry. Were you able to contact him or have contact with him through any -- in any way, through any medium, after he'd left the family home but before he came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We would sometimes call him on the phone. We even visited him once there, my father, my mother, my sister, and I to see how he was doing, because we missed him so much. I remember the period of the bombing, when they were bombing this neighbourhood where he lived and we called him up and asked him to come over. We felt better having him close. We had gotten quite used to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you first become aware that he had been arrested and brought to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: He called us on the phone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you knew nothing about his arrest until he contacted you from The Hague by telephone. I take it that's affirmative. Now, since he's been in The Hague, what sort of --

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since he's been in the United Nations Detention Centre in The Hague, what sort of contact have you been able to have with him? First of all, other than personal visits, what sort of contact have you had?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Leaving aside personal visits, i.e. visits to The Hague, what sort of contact have you had with him and how have you had contact with him whilst he's been in the Detention Centre?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Right. Right. I understood now. We have daily contact by telephone. He calls, and he writes, and we write to him. And sometimes if a day passes without him calling, because he doesn't have a telephone card, we get worried. We start wondering if he's all right, if everything's fine with him. And that means a lot to us, and his letters mean a lot to us. We try hard to give him our support, and we miss him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you know he has pleaded guilty to the indictment containing serious charges, don't you?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bearing in mind your relationship with him as a - and I'm not being impolite when I say this - a relatively young female, have you any concept as to how he came to act as he did, bearing in mind the man that you know?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- have you noticed, because you seem to have, from your evidence, very regular contact with him -- have you noticed any difference in his general attitude and demeanour between the times before he pleaded guilty and the times after he pleaded guilty?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that he felt great relief when it was all over, and we are happy for him. All we care about is that he be well. The only thing is I didn't quite understand whether you asked me about any difference between the moment when he arrived here and now. Rather, have I noticed any change since then?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that -- if that's a matter you can assist us with, please do. Have you noticed such a change? And if so, what was it?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: We were afraid there might be a change after the initial state of shock. We feared that it would not be the man we know, in view of the circumstances, his circumstances. However, the first time we came here to visit, my sister and I, we were happy to see that he remained the same, normal man, the man that we know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think in the time that he's been at the Detention Centre, you've been able to visit him on two occasions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It seems, from your evidence, that you have been a person who has been very supportive of him in your personal contacts with him. I may be asking a very obvious question, but is it your intention to continue with that level of support for the future?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. And I will be happy if I'm able to help him, and I'm speaking not only for myself but for my entire family, because after all, he lived with us for rather a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance. If you'd wait there, there may be some more questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrison. May I ask the Prosecution, are there any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, would you give us a few moments just to consider whether questions should be asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Yapa, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Questioned by Mr. Yapa:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm sorry I have to ask a few questions from you. You are distressed at the moment. But it is in respect of the evidence you have given in chief.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Yapa please speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm sorry that you are in a distressed position at the moment, but I have to ask you a few questions in respect of the evidence that you have given in chief. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you have -- on your testimony, it appears that you had a very, very close relationship with the -- with Mr. Dragan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, here came -- he came to your residence in Belgrade from Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know why he came?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Why did he come?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Because we invited him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You invited him when he was in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was the invitation extended, please?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: We had fears regarding his safety. We wanted to give him support.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the -- why do you speak of safety? If you please, can you explain. Why did you fear for his safety?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: We were afraid that something might happen to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, I have to repeat the question. It's not clear. When you say "something might happen to him," because of what?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that he did not feel safe there. He was in poor health. His health was equally poor when he came to stay with us. He had been wounded during the war. And as a matter of fact, he injured his spine while he was staying with us. He could not move for a few days. He could not get up at all. He could not even go to the toilet. My father helped him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not sure whether I understand you correctly, but let me get to another point. Did you know before he came that he had some responsibility in a camp called the Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: I only heard about that from the family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it to say, then, that in your frequent conversations with him, that he never discussed with you about the Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. No. Definitely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you know that there was an indictment against him at the time that he was residing with you?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. While he was residing with us in Batajnica you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In --

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Belgrade; yes?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you knew that there was an indictment against him. Your answer, please, witness. You knew that he -- there was an indictment against him?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you address him when he was with you? How did all your family members address him?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What name did you call him by, a relationship or what name did you call him by?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Dobrica. That was our nickname for him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: It is a personal name, but it also means a very good person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your -- in the course of the conversations, the close conversations that you had with him, did you also know that he had a false identity?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Did I know that he had a false identity?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that was my question. Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand this question. I only knew him as Dobrica, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you also said that when he was there, that he was extremely helpful to your family.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the family members, you yourself and the others, were attached to him.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Quite attached. Quite attached. We were attached to him, and he was attached to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: That will be all, Your Honours. Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Only one question: Do you know the name Vidovic, Deputy Chair Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Dobrica Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who would be this person?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: Dobrica. Dobrica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be -- I heard from the interpretation booth that it could be used as a kind of nickname and it means at the same time a good person. So it would be a given name. What was the name of Dobrica, the full name he used at that time?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA RIKANOVIC
utterances.text: We still call him Dobrica until the present day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. I have no further questions. Judge Agius? This is not the case. Any further questions? Then we have to thank you for coming to The Hague, giving us your testimony. And we wish you a safe trip back home to your country. You are excused. May I ask the usher, please, to guide the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask now, Mr. Morrison, what is your intention how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm going to, with Your Honours' indulgence, adopt the course, the alternative course that was canvassed this morning of not calling Mr. Nikolic at this moment but calling him, as it were, prior to have closing proceedings of the Defence case. He will give testimony, and he will therefore, of course, even at that stage - and he understands this - be liable to be asked any questions that are thought appropriate. That being the -- the case, there is nothing further that the Defence wish to put before the Trial Chamber today. All other matters are going to be reserved until the final and closing speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But we have to clarify some issues. Attached to your sentencing brief, we find Annex B and Annex C. Is it your intention to tender one of those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is. I was going to deal with those matters in a global sense at the conclusion of the case. That was my intention. If Your Honour has another way that you wish it to be done, I would be pleased to cooperate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's necessary before hearing the final arguments of both parties to know what is in evidence and what is not. Therefore, we have to decide today on this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: So be it. The statements at Annex B consist of the following: The first is Milica Nikolic; she is the defendant's mother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. May I ask the Prosecution: Related to this statement of Milica Nikolic, are there any objections? Is there a need of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Your Honour, so far as the contents of that statement goes, it appears that it is more in relation to the character of Mr. Dragan Nikolic. So that extent, we would not be having any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then this document is admitted into evidence as Exhibit 4. Correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit D1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We can also call it D1. There is no problem. D1. Please continue. What about the next statement, Fikret Zukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's the evidence of Fikret Zukic, nicknamed Like. Again, that's a short, self-evident statement, and the Defence wish to simply tender it for the purposes of its contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, in respect of this statement, we have a serious concern. Your Honours will be pleased to see in the penultimate paragraph there is a statement to the effect that he did not cause any incidents. Now, that goes beyond speaking of his character, and it is contrary to the plea tendered by the accused, by Mr. Nikolic. He did not cause any incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the purpose of this statement is not to suggest that he didn't cause any incidents at Susica. That would be nonsense. He's pleaded guilty to the indictment. The plain reading of the statement is this: "I knew Dragan Nikolic" - past tense - "as a person not inclined to violence. He did not cause any incidents, he always associated with persons of all nationalities and religious beliefs." It can plainly only relate to his behaviour before Susica. And that's the purpose to which it is tendered. It's not suggested that it otherwise applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Having heard the parties on this, and having briefly conferred, this statement is admitted into evidence as document D2 for the reasons that admission into evidence does not mean any kind of assessment of the content of the statement. The weight attached to such a document will be decided by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's now turn to the next document, a statement of Majstorovic Milenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Again, that is the statement of someone who knew Dragan Nikolic and speaks of his acquaintanceship before the war and speaks of his acquaintanceship and companionship before the war and his work at the -- it says "Azpro." I think that must be a typographical error. It must be Alpro. There are then some personal observations, which obviously have very limited evidential weight from Mr. Milenko. And for the most part -- well, really the whole of the purpose of the statement is to underline his character before the conflict and simply to, in the penultimate paragraph on page 1, to point out that for Dragan Nikolic's brother it was very hard to understand the accusations. Again, that's not a matter, I don't think, of any dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before I hear the Prosecution on this, I wanted to re-emphasise that document D2 was admitted into evidence, taking into account that it does not go to prove a matter of the acts and conduct of the accused. So may I hear the Prosecution on the next statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I thank Your Honour. This is before Your Honours as a statement of the mother of Mr. Dragan Nikolic. We have no intention of cross-examining this witness. We do not want the witness before. And we don't have any objections to the admission of this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then this statement is admitted as D3 into evidence. We now turn to Annex C.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the purpose of this annex was simply to show that there was in fact an incident in Vlasenica in March of 1995 as a result of which Dragan Nikolic was injured and suffered the injuries set out in the Court findings. I don't imagine that the fact of the incident is contentious, bearing in mind it's a matter which is easily verifiable through the court records. The only object is -- of putting that in was if it is going to be of moment to the Court, the reasoning why he might have left Vlasenica. That was one factor. As I understand it, the reasoning behind the defendant's leaving of Vlasenica in 1996 is not a matter which weighs with the Tribunal. I will be corrected if I am wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So in conclusion, you don't want to tender these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: If I am correct in my understanding, no, I don't need to tender the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Anything else you want to tender, to add to your case related to the sentencing, assisting the Trial Chamber in determining the appropriate sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: With the caveat, of course, that you already indicated that it's your intention to call your client as a witness at a later point in time. And I can't see no objections by the Prosecution to doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: For completeness, I'll deal also with the certificate, which is right at the end of Annex C, which is simply a certificate which is -- I think it's a matter which is agreed as between the Prosecutor and the Defence, but prior to his plea in this case there was no criminal record relating to Dragan Nikolic. That simply underscores that. I see nods across the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's an agreed fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: It is an agreed fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can we take it, Mr. Yapa? Just for the record, it's not reflected on the record, Mr. Yapa's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: We do agree that there is no prior report of any criminal activities. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: So subject to the caveat that Your Honour has already identified -- that is the calling of Dragan Nikolic to amplify matters of concern to this Trial Chamber, which I do not wish to deal with before he gives his testimony -- what will remain is a closing address by the Defence, which will not raise any new issues but simply, I hope, underscore and amplify the issues which are already before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It should be re-emphasised that apart from the formal testimony, no doubt the accused, Mr. Dragan Nikolic, enjoys the right to have the final word without any questioning by the parties, whatever he wants to tell the Judges, he is entitled to do so at the very end of the case. As I said earlier, with the caveats expressed, Dr. Grosselfinger is prepared to start and to give her -- as a summary of the report we all have read already before at quarter past 12.00. The trial therefore stands adjourned until 15 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just clarify something - I am sorry - before you rise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Is -- I emphasise, this is purely for personal convenience, because of another meeting that I'm going to this afternoon. Is it the Trial Chamber's intention to rise today at 1.00 or 1.30?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have to stop at 1.00 because Judge Agius has to continue with his case, so it was only an exception yesterday. However, the intention is to have this 65 ter (I) meeting as soon as possible. And may I know, did you already check whether it's -- would be feasible for you to have this hearing, say, at 2.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: For a Rule 65 ter meeting in this case at 2.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, I think that would be perfectly feasible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would it be convenient for the Prosecution as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: No inconvenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then may I also ask the registrar to be prepared to participate in this meeting in order to take minutes. So once again, the trial stays adjourned until quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
