utterances.text: Please be seated. Before we start, we just this moment received, if I see it correctly, an addendum to the report of the Max Planck Institute. And as it's a matter of time, we will hear the expert already tomorrow. The first copies before they are officially filed, may we please -- one copy per party, may we distribute it right now. May I ask the usher to give one copy to both parties. I learnt that we later on would get a full updated version. It's now on to exchange some pages where there is new research done, going in far more details of the sentencing practice. I think we can continue now. May I ask the usher to escort Madam Dr. Grosselfinger into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Madam Grosselfinger, may I first ask you to give the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly swear -- I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And in addition, I have -- please be seated. The Bench has to thank you for volunteering today. We all know that your testimony was scheduled only for Thursday, but you were flexible and kind enough to be prepared to give us a short summary of your expertise today, of course with the caveat: Should there be any question, you would need to go back to your fundamental documents, then we would call you again on Thursday. But we appreciate that you are working really on this ad hoc basis in this ad hoc Tribunal. Thank you for the flexibility, and the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: NANCY GROSSELFINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would like to draw to your attention first that the report which that you have provided me a copy of my submission is not complete in that neither the appendices, the indices at the end, nor the amended table of contents and the subsequent submission of Annex number 6 is not present, that is, Annex number 6 is considered relevant documents which I consulted in the process of the preparation of this report. It's approximately a page and a half single spaced and it consists of largely relevant UN documents. And I must say that I -- well, they were at the tail end. I consider them not the least important, but perhaps amongst the most important because they framed the line of my study, my inquiry, and therefore I would certainly want you to be having them in your possession when you're making your deliberations, and perhaps those who are going to be questioning me would also want to have them because I don't consider them less important, I consider them actually amongst the most important things included in the -- in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Absolutely. And there should be not the slightest doubt that the parties and the three Judges read -- have already read in great detail, your report, including all appendices. It is only due to the fact that it was more or less ad hoc that I provided you with this, and may I ask the usher to give also the annex to the expert. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NANCY GROSSELFINGER
utterances.text: Good. Okay. I feel much better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We appreciate it. So, please.

utterances.speaker: NANCY GROSSELFINGER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not sure exactly how you'd like me to proceed, if you'd like me to go through the relevant parts of the report, or how is it you'd like to carry on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Taking into account that we all have read your report, it would be the best if you would highlight those parts you think are of utmost important, and in short, to summarise your report.

utterances.speaker: NANCY GROSSELFINGER
utterances.text: Well, I think I should perhaps start with the manner in which I came to know this case more fully. After having read the relevant documents of the pleading and the transcript of the pleading hearing, I proceeded to go to the Detention Unit to speak with the accused for approximately 9 hours inside of the Detention Unit, on a period of two different days within the same week. I was assisted by interpreters in this endeavour, and received cooperation from the institutional staff to the maximum, as well as to the accused. At the outset, my discussions with the accused started in a personal way in order to put him in a capacity to cooperate and to understand what was expected of him in this endeavour. We spoke initially about his personal life, which is reflected in the latter portion of the report. We began with the history of his family, the people who reared him and influenced him in his early years, in considerable detail. Then we talked about his own personal, his individual experience, his schooling, where he went to school, how he adjusted inside of his community. Then we moved into adulthood, which was really the bulk of our time, and focussed on his relationships in the community, his conflicts, if any, within the community. My concern was to see if there was in his previous experience by his own definition a combative difficult personality, if he was in constant conflict or if he was politically involved, what were his values, what was moving him. To be candid, I did not find anything particularly fruitful there. The other thing I did query him about somewhat and subsequently, very much more sternly was about the consumption of alcohol and the role that alcohol played in his life, other health factors as well; his religious affiliation and the depth of his religious affiliation; his intensity of community involvement and what did that actually mean, and basically uncovered that he was going to work most of the day and enjoying himself the rest of the evening without really engaging in deep community affairs. One of the things that came out which was important was the impact of the loss of his father early in his life and the burden that it placed upon him, the pressure that he felt, his worry about his ability to contribute financially to his family, and his stepping aside or making space for his sister to take his -- what financial opportunities or work opportunities were available to him. Then we moved to the more difficult areas, which were discussing the instant offences. And our framework was the fact that he had already pled guilty to these offences, and one would not, therefore, expect him to dispute his culpability. I was looking to see further if he had previous relationship with any of these individuals, what was the basis of the relationship, and if there was any animus that existed that he could identify, that he could explain. And we went one by one with the name of every single person. He did have recognition of many of these persons, as the report would indicate.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down a little for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. He did have recognition of a conflict with one particular individual, but absent that, we could find no strong grounds for picking on these people or selecting them out. I also queried him very strongly about his eating, sleeping, and drinking habits during the course of the three months in question. I was looking to see if there were great anomalies, especially in his sleeping habits, sleep deprivation, failure to be properly fed or eating properly that would cause sugar imbalances, other kinds of organic anomalies that might contribute to judgement or failure of good judgement. And while he admitted that he drank enough and more in the evenings, he himself did not feel that -- he didn't think that it played a significant factor and did not think it was an exculpating kind of a condition. He did not attempt to avoid responsibility or taking responsibility when we discussed each of these. And I thought that was also important to recognise. We also discussed at length his movements after, how he came to know about his indictment or he didn't come to know about his indictment, and his movements and his presence in other communities. One of the things I think I was most interested in finding was his own explanation for his behaviour: Could he explain it, did he have any understanding of why he carried on as he did. He was very reflective in this moment. He told me that he had thought about it an awful lot, and that he really could not explain to himself why he had done what he had done without saying he didn't do it; agreeing he had done it, but that it represented a dark side of his character which he did not know previously had existed; that he acknowledged that it did in fact exist, and that he was in wonder as to where it emerged from. He was -- seemed to be genuinely befuddled as to what the explanation for such behaviour could be, almost looking to me for offering him an explanation for this in some theory or something he thinks I might know. So then we talked about -- and over the course of the interviews, I think we had nine hours. But there were two interviews in the first week and then in the second week I saw him again after I had interviewed other folks in the field. And in that time, he had a chance to think. Much of our talk focussed on what could be done now, if anything. And in this, he had already done some homework and some thinking. First he acknowledged that this was -- these events were extremely grave and that in many respects whatever could be done would be very small and so late in time that perhaps those who might benefit from it or might see or hear of it might take it as sincere or serious, or too little entirely too late. So that did concern him. It concerned him in the sense that it would be seen as crocodile tears, as disingenuous, as self-seeking and self-serving, more than focussed on the needs of the persons whom he had harmed. So that part was very much in his forefront in terms of his thinking about how he could do something at this stage. We discussed possible things that could be done, some of which -- he came up with some ideas of his own. And I detail in the report his notion of how he might approach -- begin to approach persons already he believes in the Vlasenica community who are interested or have expressed concern for him, and joining with them and in a sort of a snowball approach move out from those individuals to try and discover other persons who would be willing to talk to him or accept responsibility -- some communication from him of an apologetic nature and as a means of reconciliation. One of the -- we talked about some modalities that do exist in other places. I don't know if you want me to go into the details of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary at this point in time, because it's reflected in your report, and it's for the President and the Bureau of this Tribunal later to determine what is necessary.

utterances.speaker: NANCY GROSSELFINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NANCY GROSSELFINGER
utterances.text: So other than -- we discussed also his attitude towards receiving punishment, what his punishment should be. And beyond punishment, what else he might do after the punishment phase is over. I'm not sure, Your Honours, what it is you'd like to hear from me next that is not, for instance, contained already in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you could, please, be so kind and go in some details in the way as you indicated in your report that he showed remorse, because you mentioned it already in the beginning of your report; however, we can only take into account those facts that are in evidence. We know that we will hear words from the accused himself. Nevertheless, it might be helpful if you go in some details of your discussion of his approach towards victims, the relatives.

utterances.speaker: NANCY GROSSELFINGER
utterances.text: With regard to the specific victims that were announced in the indictment, I asked him in each and every case if he felt any sorrow or remorse or regret for having harmed this particular individual. In each case, he said yes. There was one exception in which he felt that he had had some provocation, that he had received misinformation about this man's intentions towards his sister, and that operating on that he had taken on these behaviours. He subsequently realised that the man's protestations were probably accurate and that he himself, the accused, had been misled into thinking that this man was going to undertake some sexual violence against his sister. Absent that, all the others he expressed up front at the very -- at the beginning of the questioning his remorse for having harmed them. I asked him how he felt that remorse and for how long he had felt that -- that shame, that guilt, and he could go back to the beginning of those feelings from the moment that the camp was closing down. Now, initially, that started, he said, as contemplation of the possible consequences for his behaviour, but it continued to bother and haunt him and visit him. He said it intensified, especially when he went to live in Serbia. He was much on his own, and living in his own thoughts and in his own head, and then it did bother him. Mentally, he said that was probably the lowest point in all the years from the time the offences occurred until the day in which I saw him, that that was the most difficult time, and in part, because he found in his own mind no way out, no modalities for doing anything about that. He also talked about this in terms of the fact that when he came to plead, that it released in some ways a burden that he had felt, almost a double-edged sword in the sense of not just wanting the burden to be of benefit to him, because he now was feeling better, but also with a recognition that he -- well, he had -- was feeling better. He alone was not entitled to feel better but he still had a duty to the victims and the survivors to try and find a way to make them also feel better, that he just couldn't plead and have a lighter -- have a lighter conscience of it, that all the work was not yet done. When he -- we talked about -- he expressed also on several occasions willingness to meet around the table to discuss, and that was one of the ways that he was most strong, in that he wanted it not to be an experience which the victims would perceive as enforced or imposed but something that was coming genuinely from his heart and also at a time when it would not advantage him in any legal way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Agius, do you have any additional questions for the time being?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So then it would be first for the Prosecution. Do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: With Your Honours' permission, I have a few questions of Dr. Grosselfinger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And we take it that we are all aware of the caveat that if need may be, Dr. Grosselfinger has to go back to the underlying documents. So please take this into account when questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I thank Your Honour. My questions will be more general than specific, so I'm sure she'll be in a position to answer my questions. Questioned by Mr. Yapa:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Grosselfinger, I must express thanks to the report that you have submitted to at the request of Their Honours. You have done an exhaustive study. But I have a few questions about the report itself. Now, going into finding the necessary data for your report, your exercise was just a matter of gathering information; was it correct?

utterances.speaker: NANCY GROSSELFINGER
utterances.text: Well, in the sense that I was not explicitly asked to make an interpretation, yes, I mean, what's here is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, would it be correct to say that it was more or less a fact-finding mission?

utterances.speaker: NANCY GROSSELFINGER
utterances.text: Yes and no, except for one thing. I think really, Mr. Yapa, the question really is, to look at his socialisation was to look at the manner in which not only he was reared but the manner which he has conducted as an adult person, and I took that also to mean the capacity or incapacity to admit error and to see what, if anything, you could do once you've realised you've made a mistake. So I had a broad interpretation of socialisation, not just what happens to you until your parents send you out the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But now, what you have done in the report is placed the facts that you were able to gather, but you have not given, if I may say so, an opinion, an expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: NANCY GROSSELFINGER
utterances.text: I was not asked to make a recommendation or so on sentencing or anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What you would hope is that the Court will take into account the facts that you have gathered and form Their Honours' own opinion, in respect of the facts that you have found out.

utterances.speaker: NANCY GROSSELFINGER
utterances.text: Well, my assumption is that they don't know enough personal information about him. They were interested in a great deal of personal information, which would not -- has not been elaborated in other ways. So that my inquiry was to go and find out much field information that they might have been interested in knowing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. Thank you. So you ventured upon finding out from the accused as to his conduct at the camp, subsequent conduct, and conduct after the plea of guilt.

utterances.speaker: NANCY GROSSELFINGER
utterances.text: Well, maybe I wouldn't use the word "conduct." Some of it was inquiry about his whereabouts. Some of it was his own assessment of his thinking, his state of mind. Some of it was observations of other persons as to how he was behaving or what they thought they could see from outside of him. So it wasn't all -- it wasn't all conduct. Some of it was, you know, self-assessment, self-reflection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NANCY GROSSELFINGER
utterances.text: "Attitude" maybe would be a word I could use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far as Mr. Dragan Nikolic is concerned, whatever he has said now, at least most of it, is after reflection.

utterances.speaker: NANCY GROSSELFINGER
utterances.text: In the passage of time, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what I want to say is that now he reflects as to why he conducted in a particular way sometime in the past.

utterances.speaker: NANCY GROSSELFINGER
utterances.text: Well, I -- that's all I had was a snapshot of him in a two-week time frame; that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In reflecting upon the events that took place or the incidents that he took part in, he is now expressing remorse, at least he expressed so to you.

utterances.speaker: NANCY GROSSELFINGER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity of raising any questions with the victims or the witnesses in this case?

utterances.speaker: NANCY GROSSELFINGER
utterances.text: Yes, I did, actually. There were several things. First of all, the Judges explicitly told me not to contact the victims themselves, that it was their understanding that they were quite frail and concerned and distressed, and that I should not do so directly. And therefore, I did not do that. In fact, one of the ways I attempted to learn about the victims was by speaking with you, calling you, if you remember, and we had a short discussion, and after which you urged me that I should speak with the Victim/Witness Unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, there are certain matters in respect of which he has given answers in which he attempts to tell you that he himself could not understand as to why he conducted himself in relation to certain incidents at the camp.

utterances.speaker: NANCY GROSSELFINGER
utterances.text: Yes, he said it was a mystery to him to this day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the witnesses have spoken of his deliberate, voluntary acts in relation to assaults on them, and if that conduct reveals that it was not a question of his acting involuntary, that it was a voluntary conduct on his part, what would be the position?

utterances.speaker: NANCY GROSSELFINGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I think that, Mr. Yapa, I'm not in a position to challenge the integrity of any witnesses that have -- who at the time I prepared my report I've heard none of, and I wouldn't seek to undermine the veracity of their statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not questioning you on the material that you have placed, because these are in relation to the answers that you have got from the accused and the witnesses. I conclude by saying that you placed this material so that Their Honours can form their own opinion.

utterances.speaker: NANCY GROSSELFINGER
utterances.text: I didn't speak to any witnesses that I know of, Mr. Yapa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. May I omit that word, "witnesses," but you did speak to people who could speak to the antecedents of the accused, maybe the parents, other.

utterances.speaker: NANCY GROSSELFINGER
utterances.text: I didn't construe them to be witnesses in the sense of the Tribunal sense. You mean persons who --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NANCY GROSSELFINGER
utterances.text: -- who knew him, who were witness in the sense that they lived around him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Quite correct.

utterances.speaker: NANCY GROSSELFINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NANCY GROSSELFINGER
utterances.text: They were persons that claimed familiarity with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: That would be all. I thank Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Yapa. The Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. I'm particularly conscious of the time. By my watch, it's eight minutes to 1.00. I can confidently say that if I started today, I would not conclude by 1.00, and there are matters that I need to go into. I also want to contemplate the questions asked by the OTP, as I'm not fully sure that I yet understand them, or what -- the reasoning that lay behind them. Before I ask any questions, I want to make sure that I can deal with those issues in a satisfactory way. The long and the short of it is that I'm going to ask that the caveat be applied that was earlier suggested and that I have a chance to ask questions of Dr. Grosselfinger as was originally intended on Thursday of this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you be prepared to start with the line of questions today, or how shall I understand your remarks?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I must be being particularly obtuse. I'm not quite sure what Your Honour is asking. To start, as it were, the examination today and simply stop it at 1.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, because the background of the question is the following: In case there might be a very specific question from your side, it would be appropriate that the expert could be prepared, especially on this specific question, and therefore it would be appropriate to start today and then if need may be, to continue on Thursday, as scheduled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make a counter-suggestion, that I reduce into writing those questions which are likely to require Dr. Grosselfinger to fully consult her documents and make sure that she has them at the latest by tomorrow lunchtime, and I can give both yourselves and the OTP copies of those questions. They won't be the only questions I ask, but they will enable the witness to prepare so that I won't be asking questions today to which she feels she does not have a comprehensive answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's a fair suggestion, and we -- I have to repeat -- I think it's a fair suggestion, and therefore we can continue this way. Dr. Grosselfinger, you are prepared to act based on these prepared questions in writing. And of course, if there should be any additional questions, it is -- or it would be for the Prosecution either to add them on Thursday or also to put them in front of the expert witness in writing already today -- tomorrow. Sorry. So then I take it that we interrupt the examination of Dr. Grosselfinger for today. I see the tight schedule, and there are only a few minutes left. Thank you so far for today, and please be prepared to get these questions in writing tomorrow and to continue with your expert testimony on Thursday. However, I can't right now tell you when your expert testimony will be continued on Thursday, because I don't know the scope of questions put to the expert witness on sentencing. So therefore, please understand that I can't give you an exact hour when you will be called on Thursday. The same rules apply, of course; you are entitled to follow the proceedings in the public gallery during tomorrow's session. Thank you for today. May I ask the usher, please, to escort Dr. Grosselfinger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then only one final administrative matter: If I'm not absolutely wrong, we did not decide on the 94 bis report provided by Dr. Zepter, at least that is what I heard from the registrar. You have tendered this statement under Rule 94 bis by filing it. Are there any objections by the Defence related to this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. I must be wrong. I was under the impression that we had already indicated that we had no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I was under the same impression. I only learned right now that it was not yet entered into evidence. Please cross-check. And if it's not yet in evidence, then it's hereby admitted into evidence. And I take it that there is no need of any kind of cross-examination, so ... We'll announce the number when we have cross-checked the documents. Any other issues to be discussed today? I can see no submissions, no requests. So we continue with the 65 ter (I) meeting in my office at 2.00 sharp, and the trial as such stays adjourned until tomorrow, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
